publisher: Sennrich, Haddow, Birch · University of Edinburgh
title: BPE subword tokenization: how a fixed vocabulary can spell any word and where LLM tokens come from
summary: Neural translation vocabularies have only tens of thousands of words, so rare and new words can't be translated. This paper turns byte pair encoding, a 1994 compression algorithm, into a tokenization method: start from letters and repeatedly merge the most common adjacent pair. We run the paper's code by hand for 10 merges, then look at its experiments, the errors caused by inconsistent segmentation, and how it became the token behind today's large models.
ai_summary: Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units (Sennrich et al., University of Edinburgh, ACL 2016) applies byte pair encoding (BPE) to tokenization: starting from characters, it repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols, and the number of merges sets the vocabulary size. Rare and new words are represented as subword sequences, so translation no longer needs a back-off dictionary. On WMT 2015 English→German and English→Russian, the subword models beat the dictionary baseline by up to 1.1 and 1.3 BLEU, with clearly better rare-word translation and more consistent segmentation when BPE is learned jointly on both languages.
brief: Problem: translation vocabularies have only tens of thousands of words, so rare words, names, and compounds must be looked up or copied verbatim, and the model cannot generate new words.
Method: borrow the BPE compression algorithm — start from letters, repeatedly merge the most common adjacent pair, and use a fixed vocabulary to represent any word.
Result: no dictionary needed; English→German and English→Russian BLEU improves by up to 1.1 and 1.3 points, rare and unseen words translate better, and joint BPE gives more consistent segmentation.
Limits: vocabulary size is chosen heuristically; the highest BLEU comes from character bigrams, not BPE; and separate BPE can produce inconsistent splits and transliteration errors.

cover.headline: BPE subword tokenization: a close reading of the original paper
cover.highlight: A fixed vocabulary that can spell any word.

nodes.label: repeatedly merge the most common pair

sections.h: The short version: what this paper actually did

blocks.p: In August 2015, Rico Sennrich, Barry Haddow, and Alexandra Birch of the University of Edinburgh released this paper; it appeared at ACL 2016 a year later. It targets an old problem in neural machine translation: **the model's vocabulary is fixed, but the words it needs to translate are endless.**

At the time, neural translation models typically had vocabularies of only 30,000 to 50,000 words. Anything outside the vocabulary simply became an “unknown word” symbol, patched up during translation with a dictionary lookup or by copying the source word verbatim. But names, compounds, loanwords, and newly coined words keep appearing — especially in a language like German, which can fuse several words into a single long one.

The paper's answer is to **break words into smaller “subwords.”** Common words stay whole, rare words split into a few frequent pieces, and in the worst case the pieces go down to single letters. As a result, a fixed-size vocabulary can represent any word. How to split? The paper borrows a 1994 data compression algorithm, **byte pair encoding (BPE):** start from single letters and repeatedly merge the two symbols that most often appear together in the corpus into a new symbol. The number of merges determines the vocabulary size.

On the WMT 2015 English→German and English→Russian tasks, the subword model no longer needs a dictionary lookup, outperforming the dictionary baseline by up to 1.1 and 1.3 BLEU points respectively, with clearly better translations for rare words and words never seen in training.

The paper's influence goes far beyond machine translation. The **tokens** that today's GPT, LLaMA, and other large models talk about are mostly produced by BPE or its variants. What a “token” means when people say “the model reads one token at a time” took shape starting with this paper.

callout.title: One-sentence version
callout.text: BPE = start from letters and repeatedly glue the most common adjacent two pieces into one. Common words eventually become a single piece; rare words stay as a few fragments. That way a fixed-size vocabulary can spell any word.

callout.title: Three small ideas you need for this paper
callout.text: It's fine if you know nothing about them; these three are enough:
list: **Vocabulary:** the list of all symbols the model knows. The size of the model's input and output layers scales with the vocabulary size, so the vocabulary cannot be unlimited.

**Encoder–decoder translation model:** one network reads the source sentence, another writes the translation, with attention aligning the two. The model in this paper is the same one covered in our close reading of the Bahdanau attention paper.
**BLEU:** measures how much a machine translation overlaps with reference translations at the word level; higher is better.

sections.h: The problem: a closed vocabulary, an open language

blocks.p: In word-level translation models, when the model hits a word outside the vocabulary (what the paper calls OOV), the usual fix is to “back off to a dictionary”: output an unknown-word symbol, use attention to find the corresponding source word, look it up in a bilingual dictionary, and copy it verbatim if the lookup fails.

The paper points out several problems. Words in two languages do not always line up one-to-one: a German compound may correspond to several English words. Copying is reasonable for names, but often you need to change word forms or transliterate, for example from Latin to Cyrillic letters. And a word-level model simply **cannot generate** new words it never saw in training.

On the other hand, many “unknown words” are actually **transparently translatable**: a competent translator, seeing one for the first time, can still work it out from its parts. The paper gives three categories:

fig.title: Three kinds of words translatable through smaller units
fig.subtitle: Examples from Section 3 of the paper
rows: English Barack Obama → Russian Барак Обама
Same alphabet: copy; different alphabet: transliterate sound by sound.
Change a few letters by regular rules.
English solar system → German Sonnensystem (Sonne + System)
Split into morphemes, translate each, then reassemble.

blocks.p: The paper examined 100 rare tokens in the German training data (outside the 50,000 most frequent types) and found that most could be translated from English this way: 56 compounds, 21 names, 6 cognates or loanwords, 5 words translatable through affixes, plus 1 number and 1 computer language identifier.

sections.h: BPE: turning a compression algorithm into a tokenizer

blocks.p: The original BPE was a compression algorithm proposed by Gage in 1994: repeatedly find the most frequent pair of bytes in the data and replace it with an unused byte. The paper adapts it to tokenization, merging characters and character sequences instead of bytes:

list: **Initialize:** the vocabulary contains only all single characters. Each word is written as a character sequence with a special “end-of-word” symbol at the end (written as · in the paper and `</w>` in the code) so word boundaries can be restored after translation.

**Count:** count every adjacent pair of symbols. Each word is weighted by its frequency in the corpus, and pairs never cross word boundaries, so the whole algorithm runs on a word→count dictionary and is fast.
**Merge:** replace every occurrence of the most frequent pair (say A and B) with a new symbol AB, and add it to the vocabulary.
**Repeat:** return to the counting step until the predetermined number of merges is done.

blocks.p: Each merge creates a new symbol representing a character n-gram. Frequent character n-grams, and even whole frequent words, eventually merge into a single symbol. Final vocabulary size = initial characters + number of merges, and **the number of merges is the algorithm's only hyperparameter.**

At test time, split a new word into characters, then apply the learned merge rules **in the order they were learned**. Any word can be processed this way, so the vocabulary is fixed but the words it can represent are open-ended. The paper says the only unknown symbols that might appear are characters never seen in training.

callout.title: Like finding common collocations in a text
callout.text: BPE is a bit like making a book into shorthand: first you notice that “t” is most often followed by “h”, so you treat “th” as a single character; then you notice “th” is often followed by “e”, so you create “the”. High-frequency combinations keep gluing into bigger chunks until a whole common word becomes one character; low-frequency words never glue, so they stay as parts. It knows nothing about grammar — only statistics.

blocks.p: The paper includes a small Python implementation, just a dozen or so lines. We run it on its own example:

plain.title: The most frequent pair glues first
plain.text: At the start, every letter is its own piece. Count which two adjacent pieces appear together most often, then glue them into one: first e+s, then es+t, and so on. Repeated like this, common affixes (est) and common words grow into complete pieces on their own, while rare words stay split.

fig.note: The more merges, the bigger the pieces and the shorter the sequence — but the larger the vocabulary. Real use runs tens of thousands of merges.

quiz.q: What is BPE's only manually set hyperparameter?
options: The number of merges, which directly determines the final vocabulary size
The maximum number of pieces per word
How the end-of-word symbol is written
quiz.why: Final vocabulary = initial characters + one new symbol per merge. More merges mean larger common pieces and shorter text, but a larger vocabulary. The paper's English→German experiments used 59,500 merges.

sections.h: The trade-off between vocabulary size and text length

blocks.p: A tokenizer must balance two things. A larger vocabulary makes the model's input and output layers larger, which is slower and uses more memory. But a too-small vocabulary splits a word into many pieces, lengthening the sequence; encoder and decoder computation is at least linear in sequence length, and the model must carry information over longer distances.

fig.title: The same German training corpus, segmented different ways
fig.subtitle: From Table 1 of the paper. Token counts are in millions; “unknown” is the number of tokens in the development set that cannot be segmented out.
fig.note: Whole words need 1.75 million entries and still don't cover everything; single characters have no unknown words but make the text more than five times longer. BPE makes the text only about 12% longer, shrinks the vocabulary to just over 60,000, and has no unknown words.

plain.title: Bigger building blocks, fewer pieces per sentence
plain.text: The vocabulary is the set of building blocks; text length is how many blocks a sentence takes. Whole-word segmentation has so many block types it cannot fit them all, and rare words have no block at all. Character segmentation has very few types, but a sentence uses many blocks, so the sequence the model reads becomes long. Subwords sit in between.

blocks.p: The paper also tried linguistic methods: frequency-based compound splitting, rule-based syllable hyphenation, and unsupervised morpheme segmentation with Morfessor. They only modestly shrink the vocabulary and still cannot solve out-of-vocabulary words, so they don't meet the goal of no dictionary and an open vocabulary.

sections.h: Two languages: learn separately or jointly?

blocks.p: Translation involves two languages, so BPE can be learned separately on the source and target sides, or on the combined corpus of both sides — what the paper calls **joint BPE**.

list: **Learned separately:** text and vocabulary are more compact, and each subword unit is guaranteed to have appeared in that language's training text.

**Learned jointly:** the two sides are segmented more consistently. If learned separately, the same name may be split into different pieces in the two languages, making it hard for the model to learn the mapping between them.

blocks.p: How can English and Russian, with different alphabets, be learned jointly? The paper first transliterates Russian into Latin characters using ISO-9, learns BPE on the combined corpus, then transliterates the learned merge rules back into Cyrillic to apply them to Russian text.

The experiments use WMT 2015 data: the English→German training set has 4.2 million sentence pairs, about 100 million tokens; English→Russian has 2.6 million sentence pairs, about 50 million tokens. The model follows the encoder–decoder architecture from Bahdanau et al., with a 1000-dimensional hidden layer and 620-dimensional embeddings, trained with Adadelta for about 7 days and a beam width of 12. Each setting trains 8 models; the paper reports the best single model on the development set and the ensemble of all 8.

Systems compared: WUnk (word-level model that outputs an unknown symbol for out-of-vocabulary words), WDict (word-level model + back-off dictionary, the main baseline), C2-50k (the 50,000 most common words unsplit, the rest segmented into character bigrams), BPE-60k (BPE learned separately for each language), and BPE-J90k (joint BPE). None of the subword systems use a back-off dictionary.

fig.title: English→German: subword models translate rare and unseen words better
fig.subtitle: From Table 2 of the paper, newstest2015, ensemble of 8 models. BLEU and chrF3 are higher-better; the “rare words” and “unseen words” columns are unigram F1 (%).
fig.note: Rare words are those outside the 50,000 most common training-set words; unseen words never appear in training. In English→German, most unseen words are names, where copying is enough, so the dictionary baseline is actually best in this column.

fig.title: English→Russian: with different alphabets, the subword advantage is clearer
fig.subtitle: From Table 3 of the paper, newstest2015, ensemble of 8 models
fig.note: Russian uses Cyrillic, so names cannot simply be copied; they must be transliterated. The dictionary baseline's unseen-word F1 is only 6.6, while the subword model learns piece-by-piece transliteration and raises it to 18.3.

blocks.p: A few observations: every subword system has higher rare-word F1 than the baseline (English→German from 36.8% to 41.8%, English→Russian from 26.5% to 29.7%); ensemble BLEU is 0.3 to 1.3 points higher than the baseline; and joint BPE is better than separate BPE on most metrics. The paper also cautions that rare words, though only a small part of the test set, often carry the core information of a sentence, so overall metrics like BLEU likely understate their impact.

**Frequency analysis.** The paper groups translated words by their frequency rank in the training set. For the 50,000 most common words, all systems perform similarly. For words ranked between 50,000 and 500,000, performance degrades sharply with frequency if they are kept as whole words in the vocabulary, while subword systems stay far more stable. The reason is sparsity: in training, the 50,000th-ranked word appears only 60 times, and the 500,000th appears only twice, too little to learn well — while subword pieces are far more frequent. So **shrinking the vocabulary and representing more words as subwords can actually be better.**

fig.title: How the subword model translates unseen words
fig.subtitle: From Tables 4 and 5 of the paper. “|” marks a subword boundary.

list: **“Wrong” splits can still translate correctly:** BPE segmentation doesn't always respect morpheme boundaries. For example, BPE-60k splits “research institute” into `Forsch|ungsinstitu|ten`, while `Forschungs|instituten` would be more linguistically natural, but the translation still comes out correct. The character bigram system splits “research institute” into a dozen or more pieces and still gets this part right (though its translation also drops “health”). The paper says the model is robust to over-splitting.

**Inconsistent segmentation causes errors:** when BPE is learned separately, BPE-60k's transliteration of `rakfisk` ends up with an extra `п` and a missing `к`. The paper traces this to words whose two sides are split differently in the training data (for example `p|rak|ri|ti` versus `пра|крит|и`), so the model wrongly learns `rak → пра`. Joint BPE keeps the splits consistent on both sides, so this problem disappears.

**With too little data, transliteration can go wrong:** `asinine` (“foolish”) should be translated as `dumm`; the subword model produced something like `Asinin-Situation`. Wrong, but a plausible loanword guess.

**The opening example is misspelled:** the paper opens with the German compound `Abwasser|behandlungs|anlange` (“sewage water treatment plant”). The correct spelling is `Abwasserbehandlungsanlage`; the last segment has an extra n.

**Figure 1 and the code use different examples:** the Algorithm 1 code runs on `low`, `lower`, `newest`, `widest`, while Figure 1 shows merges learned from `low`, `lowest`, `newer`, `wider`. The body text's claim that “the unseen word lower is split into low er·” refers to the Figure 1 example. Running the code directly won't reproduce Figure 1.

**The “9–11%” figures disagree with the tables:** the text says rare words make up only 9% to 11% of the test set. According to the counts in Tables 2 and 3, English→German is 2900 / 44085, about 6.6%; English→Russian is 5442 / 55654, about 9.8%. The discrepancy may come from different counting conventions, but the paper doesn't say.

**The best BLEU was not from BPE:** for the English→German ensemble, the highest BLEU (25.3) came from the character bigram system; BPE-60k's single model BLEU (21.5) was even below the dictionary baseline (22.0). The paper's main evidence is the rare-word F1 and chrF3, not BLEU.

**The vocabulary size was picked by rule of thumb:** the paper admits the number of merges was chosen “somewhat arbitrarily,” mainly to remain comparable with earlier work. Automatically selecting the best vocabulary size is left for future research.

sections.h: Afterward: where today's LLM tokens come from

blocks.p: BPE quickly became the standard first step for neural text processing. Several papers in Thread One are built on it:

fig.title: How models in Thread One segment text
fig.subtitle: From the data processing sections of each paper
rows: BPE, with a shared source/target vocabulary
WordPiece (a subword method similar in spirit to BPE)
BPE (via SentencePiece), numbers split into single digits, unknown characters fall back to bytes

list: **Byte-level BPE:** GPT-2 points out that doing BPE over Unicode characters requires an initial vocabulary of more than 130,000, while typical BPE vocabularies have only 32,000 to 64,000 entries. At the **byte** level, the initial vocabulary is only 256 symbols, and any string can be represented, including Chinese and emoji. It also forbids BPE merges across character categories; otherwise it would learn duplicate tokens such as `dog.` `dog!` `dog?`.

**Numbers split into single digits:** LLaMA splits all numbers into individual digits. The paper doesn't explain why; the common interpretation is that it makes digit segmentation more regular, avoiding irregular chunks such as “1234” being split into “12”“34”, which is friendlier for arithmetic.
**Tokens determine what the model “sees”:** context length, per-token pricing, and the strange mistakes models make when counting letters or doing arithmetic all trace back to tokenization.

blocks.p: The next paper in this thread returns to vision to look at another building block: **residual connections** (ResNet), which make networks with hundreds of layers trainable.

sections.h: Check yourself: did you get it?

quiz.q: With BPE, what happens to an English word never seen during training?
options: It is split into learned subword pieces: in the worst case down to single letters, and it can always be represented.
It has to be looked up in a dictionary.
quiz.why: At test time, the word is first split into characters, then the learned merge rules are applied in order. As long as every character has been seen, the word can always be represented — that's exactly what “open vocabulary” means.

quiz.q: Why not just use single characters as the vocabulary and eliminate unknown words altogether?
options: The text becomes very long (about 5.5 times longer than whole words in Table 1), computation grows, and the model must pass information over much longer distances.
quiz.why: Encoder–decoder computation is at least linear in sequence length. BPE strikes a balance between vocabulary size and sequence length: a vocabulary of just over 60,000, with text only about 12% longer.

quiz.q: In the English→Russian experiments, why is joint BPE better than learning BPE separately for the two languages?
options: The two sides are segmented more consistently, so the same name is split into corresponding pieces in the two languages and the model can learn piece-by-piece transliteration more easily.
quiz.why: When learned separately, `rakfisk` came out with an extra letter and a missing letter because the two sides were segmented inconsistently in the training data. Joint BPE first transliterates Russian into Latin letters, learns the merges on both sides together, and so keeps the segmentation consistent.

blocks.p: After reading this, you should be able to answer the following:

list: What problems do word-level translation models have with rare words? Why is a back-off dictionary not enough?
What are BPE's four steps, and why add an end-of-word symbol?
Why is the number of merges the only hyperparameter? How does it affect vocabulary size and text length?
How does BPE handle a new word at test time?
What are the benefits of joint BPE and of learning BPE separately?
Why can shrinking the vocabulary and representing more words as subwords sometimes be better?
What problem does GPT-2's byte-level BPE solve?
